item.title: Code Lifespan Survival Analysis (CLSA): Predicting the Survival of Source Code Lines Using AST-Aware Mining
item.description: arXiv:2606.04993v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Superseded by arXiv:2611.10530. Context: Predicting which source lines will be deleted - and when - matters for maintenance and review prioritization. Existing MSR approaches work at file or method granularity, masking individual-statement risk. Objective: We introduce Code Lifespan Survival Analysis (CLSA), the first framework to model individual-line deletion risk from covariates - where prior line-granularity work estimated lifespans but found no significant predictors. CLSA treats each line as a right-censored subject and estimates deletion risk from structural, contextual, and temporal covariates; its strongest predictors are computable statically from one file (AST structure plus line token count), without version history or bug data. Method: We mine 32.5 million line birth events from 120 open-source TypeScript repositories. A 5-stage matching pipeline separates true deletions from refactoring noise, preventing 8.3 million false deaths. We fit a Cox Proportional Hazards model with 15 covariates and check robustness via Weibull/Log-Logistic AFT, gamma frailty, and time-stratified landmark models. Results: The Kaplan-Meier median survival time is 1,335-1,352 days (about 3.7 years), verified on the full 32.5-million-line population and an independent resample; among deleted lines the median lifespan is 95.7 days. Line token count is a steady protective factor (HR=0.87) that stays essentially flat with age (HR 0.89-0.91 across regimes). Lines in conditional branches show no detectable effect at birth (HR=0.98, 0-90 days, not significant) but become a risk factor after 90 days (HR=1.23). Repository identity is the largest factor: a gamma frailty model (variance theta=1.451) raises concordance from 0.587 to 0.676. Conclusion: Line-level survival modeling is tractable, yielding interpretable risk signals and a calibration recipe for time-conditional scoring in IDEs and code review.
item.dc:creator: Pavel Gurov

item.title: AI Writes Faster Than Humans Can Review: A Longitudinal Study of an Enterprise 2x Mandate
item.description: arXiv:2607.01904v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enterprises increasingly mandate the use of AI coding tools and set ambitious productivity targets, yet there is little longitudinal evidence on whether such productivity targets have been reached, how, and at what cost. We present a quantitative case study of a documented enterprise "2x" mandate: in June 2025, the CTO of a mid-sized, AI-forward software company set the goal of doubling merged pull requests (PRs) per engineer with AI. Using a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 PRs (Jan 2024-Apr 2026), we estimate the effect of AI adoption by comparing each developer's PR throughput after they started using AI tools with their throughput before adoption. We find that the company eventually reached the target, but only in the tenth month and not in the way the mandate implied: PR throughput barely changed at the mandate date, increased by about 12% when each developer started using AI, and then kept increasing as developers accumulated use. The target was not met merely by working longer or splitting work: extra working days account for at most one-fifth of the throughput increase, and the added PRs became larger and skewed toward features and bug fixes rather than routine changes. The gain is similar across seniority levels and larger in repositories created since 2022. The cost of AI adoption fell on code review, where load per reviewer doubled and automated review exceeded human review in coverage within months of the mandate. We interpret these results as strong evidence that the adoption and sustained usage of AI raises PR throughput in an enterprise setting, with two caveats: throughput is only a proxy for productivity, and the exact size of the effect remains uncertain due to a lack of truly randomized assignment in our setting. Our results have implications for organizations under AI transformations and researchers studying the impact of AI on software development productivity.
item.dc:creator: Hao He, Shyam Agarwal, Yegor Denisov-Blanch, Pavel Azaletskiy, Sanmi Koyejo, Bogdan Vasilescu

item.title: Writing Bug Reports for Software Repair Agents: What Information Matters Most?
item.description: arXiv:2607.09553v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Software development is increasingly moving toward agentic-first workflows. This includes AI agents responsible for generating initial fixes for submitted issue reports. In this setting, issue reports are no longer merely documentation for human maintainers; they become the primary task specification for the agent. However, little is known about how such reports should be written to maximize the agent's chances of producing a correct fix. We study what makes a bug report agent-ready. Starting from the SWE-Bench Verified benchmark (i.e. a collection of 500 real repository issues with human-written gold patches and test suites for evaluating generated fixes) we manually classify each issue by change type (e.g. bug fix vs refactoring) and annotate each sentence with its information type, such as observed behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps, localization cues, and suggested fixes. We focus on the 441 issues representing bug reports, and we run on them mini-swe-agent using three LLM backbones (i.e. GPT-5-mini, MiniMax M2.5, and Gemini 3 Flash). We then fit a binomial regression model to estimate the incremental association between each information type and agent success, controlling for confounding factors. Our results suggest that agentic-first reports benefit most from information that narrows the agent's search and repair space. Suggested fixes, expressed either in code or natural language, show the strongest positive associations with pass probability, while localization cues show positive but non-significant associations. An ablation study removing selected information types confirms that agents benefit less from information traditionally useful to humans, such as reproduction steps, and more from sentences that expose a repair direction.
item.dc:creator: Vincenzo Luigi Bruno, Alessandro Giagnorio, Daniele Bifolco, Leon Wienges, Massimiliano Di Penta, Gabriele Bavota

item.title: Ninada: Sub-Clause Split-Graph VITS Streaming and Capability-Routed 24 kHz Speech Synthesis Across Twelve Scripts
item.description: arXiv:2611.10035v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: End-to-end VITS text-to-speech models synthesize natural speech in a single forward pass, yet standard ONNX exports execute monolithically over an entire clause, delaying Time-To-First-Audio (TTFA) to several seconds and spiking activation memory. Client-side deployment across Indic scripts faces four further bottlenecks: 138.8 MB float32 checkpoints per language strain browser caches, mobile WebGPU stalls for 6-14 s compiling convolution shaders while still running slower than real time ($1.44\times$ RTF), small WebAssembly pthread pools stall at barriers on big-LITTLE mobile CPUs, and mobile Web Audio pipelines drop frames or mute output under AudioWorklet contention and iOS WKWebView rules. We present Ninada, an open-source 24 kHz TTS system covering English, Classical Sanskrit, and ten Indian languages (sa, en, hi, kn, mr, bn, ta, te, ml, gu, pa, or) across a capability-routed 48-checkpoint fleet: 24 studio HiFi-GAN v1 specialists (27.9 MB W8A32+FP16 ONNX) for desktop/WebGPU and 24 distilled c8c8_384 iSTFTNet specialists (21.7 MB ONNX, $2.64\times$ fewer vocoder MACs via an exact NOLA dual-window ConvTranspose1d inverse STFT with zero complex ops) for mobile WASM, plus a 0.0 MB zero-dependency Klatt fallback. At runtime, Ninada splits a single ONNX file in memory in $< 15$ ms into prior, flow, and windowed vocoder sub-sessions streaming 12-frame halos with raised-cosine crossfades. On $N = 480$ held-out 24 kHz studio utterances, Ninada achieves 3.22 dB 0-8 kHz MCD (3.09 dB mobile iSTFTNet; 1.33 dB 24-voice distillation MCD, vs. 5.17 dB for the 1,526.8 MB 16 kHz Meta MMS fleet) and 6.07 dB 8-12 kHz error, delivering 89-155 ms audible startup on desktop WebGPU and 538-649 ms zero-underrun streaming at 0.75-0.76x RTF on a physical Google Pixel 10 Pro XL.
item.dc:creator: Hemanth HM

item.title: Characterising divergence between heuristic and language-model ratings of mobile user interface quality
item.description: arXiv:2609.05423v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated assessment of mobile user interface quality is attractive because manual review does not scale, and large language models are increasingly proposed for the task. Whether their ratings correspond to those produced by established rule-based heuristics has not been characterised at scale. We construct a 15,000-screen corpus from the RICO dataset using six documented filters, score every screen with a literature-grounded heuristic scorer, and collect ratings from three open-weight language models across two input representations, yielding 270,000 ratings. We report linearly weighted Cohen's kappa with bootstrap confidence intervals, offset-corrected kappa, intraclass correlation, and Bland-Altman limits of agreement, together with a chance baseline for the tolerance-band agreement rule. Agreement between the two rating sources is consistently weak: raw kappa falls below 0.15 in seventeen of eighteen model-representation-dimension cells. However, fifteen of eighteen cells are statistically distinguishable from zero, and correcting for a constant offset raises five cells above 0.15, so the divergence is better described as a combination of systematic bias and weak covariation than as absence of relationship. Model ratings track structural properties of the interface, but substantially less strongly than the heuristic does, and more strongly from an untruncated structural element list than from a screenshot. We further show that dimensions elicited in a single generated response are correlated by construction, reaching rho = 0.97 in one condition, which constrains what such designs can measure. We report these results as a characterisation of divergence between two automated raters rather than as evidence that either is correct, and we set out the validation a stronger claim would require.
item.dc:creator: Md Rejaul Korim Sadi, Golam Mostofa Naeem, Toufiqur Rahman Tasin, Syed Mostofa Moosa, Mahmudul Hasan Emon, Mahmudur Rashid, Ferdus Ahmed

item.title: Measuring Tabular Data Formats Cold: A Replicated Cold-Cache Benchmark of Serialization, Scan, and Index Performance on Real Datasets
item.description: arXiv:2611.10398v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Choosing a file format for tabular data is a routine engineering decision, yet published comparisons often time reads served from the operating-system page cache, use one session, or rely on a single synthetic dataset. This article benchmarks fifteen format and access-path configurations (CSV, JSON Lines, Pickle, Feather, Parquet, ORC, DuckDB, and SQLite, with several access paths) on two real public datasets, New York City taxi trips and United States airline on-time records, at 50,000 to 3 million rows. Every measurement uses an explicitly cold cache, randomized execution order, and three independent sessions (with restarts on the laptop), and is analyzed with bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted permutation tests. Parquet answered a filtered aggregation 2.6 to 11 times faster than CSV, while JSON Lines was 10 to 27 times slower. A secondary index made SQLite queries 2.6 to 4.8 times slower on randomly ordered data and helped only on data sorted by the filtered column, at low selectivity. A row filter inside the Parquet reader was significantly faster than a projected scan on flight data from one million rows and on both datasets at three million, and row-group skipping needs several row groups, which the default writer produced only at 3 million rows. A 4 GB Linux host ran out of memory on configurations that a 24 GB laptop completed and reversed some orderings, such as Pickle versus Parquet. Code, derived data, and raw timings are released.
item.dc:creator: Asra Fathima, Kristoffer Roberts
